## 1. Introduction

::: lede
Corner betting markets rate teams on how many corners they win and
concede. But the number of corners a team takes depends a lot on the
scoreline and on how strong the opponent is, and over a short run of
fixtures those two things skew the raw counts. This project removes that
bias by valuing every corner in the context it was won and builds team
ratings from the adjusted values.
:::

::: stat-row
::: stat
[`{python} n_leagues`]{.num} [leagues modelled]{.lbl}
:::

::: stat
[`{python} n_matches`]{.num} [matches]{.lbl}
:::

::: stat
[`{python} n_corners`]{.num} [corner events valued]{.lbl}
:::

::: stat
[+`{python} f"{roi_lo:.1f}"`--`{python} f"{roi_hi:.1f}"`%]{.num}
[handicap ROI, every tested rating set]{.lbl}
:::
:::

**Summary**

-   Game state has a large effect on corners. In the median league, the
    home side's share of corners is `{python} f"{med_spread:.0f}"`
    points higher when losing than when winning.
-   Over short time periods, teams can spend disproportionate amounts of
    time in winning or losing positions, so raw corner counts become
    skewed by game state effects.
-   Valuing each corner by its game state, its home/away context and the
    pre-match supremacy, and dropping "repeater" corners, gives ratings
    that predict future corners better than raw counts do at every
    window length tested.
-   Against real Pinnacle prices, the adjusted ratings are profitable in
    the **corner handicap market** across all 8 rating sets tested. The
    best rating set had an ROI of 4.1% across 3,486 bets during the
    testing window. They show **no edge in predicting corner totals**.
-   The optimal ratings framework derived from this testing now powers
    an active betting model. An automated workflow scrapes upcoming
    fixtures, derives current team ratings, makes predictions and
    compares this to the current Pinnacle prices. These predictions are
    sent to a dashboard that shows me recommended bets each day.

## 2. The data

Two scrapers feed the model. Each runs automatically every day on GitHub
Actions. The raw output is archived, and the processing stages read from
there.

### totalcorner.com: match events

The first scraper collects every finished match in `{python} n_leagues`
leagues from totalcorner.com. Each match has:

-   **an event timeline:** every goal, corner and card, with the minute
    it happened
-   **full-time match stats:** corners, shots on and off target,
    attacks, dangerous attacks and possession for each side
-   **pre-match betting lines** shown on the match page: the Asian
    handicap, goal line and corner line, with their odds

Results are stored in a local database and exported as one CSV per
league. The same scraper also collects upcoming fixtures for the live
model.

A sample of the raw output (one row per event) for Aston Villa 2--0 West
Ham on 22 March 2026. It shows 10 of the 34 columns:

```{python}
tc = load("sample_totalcorner_events.csv", dtype=str)
tc_view = tc[["Date", "Home", "Away", "Team", "Minute", "Event",
              "Home.Corners", "Away.Corners", "AH.Line", "Goal.Line"]].head(10)
table(tc_view)
```

**How it's used.** The timeline gives the scoreline at every minute of
every match. From this we can work out how long each team spent winning,
drawing and losing, and which game state each corner was won in. The
pre-match handicap and goal lines are converted into each match's
expected goals and **supremacy** (the expected goal difference), a
market-implied measure of the relative strength of each team.

```{python}
code_link("code/odds_to_goals.py", "Odds to expected goals and supremacy")
```

**Why it's useful.** Most corner data only gives team and match totals.
That can't tell you whether a team's corners came while chasing a game
or while protecting a lead. The minute-by-minute timeline is what makes
the game-state adjustments possible, and its coverage of second-tier
leagues means promoted and relegated teams can be tracked across
divisions.

### Pinnacle: corner market prices

```{python}
pc = load("pinnacle_coverage.csv").iloc[0]
pin_first = pd.to_datetime(pc["first"]).strftime("%B %Y")
pin_last = pd.to_datetime(pc["last"]).strftime("%B %Y")
pin_n = f"{pc['matches']:,}"
```

The second scraper visits Pinnacle once a day and records prices for
every fixture in the next seven days: match result, Asian handicap, goal
line, and the two corner markets (**corner handicap** and **corner
totals**). A processing step then removes Pinnacle's margin and fits a
Poisson distribution (totals) and a Skellam distribution (handicap) to
find the implied corner total and supremacy.

The archive covers `{python} pin_n` matches scraped since
`{python} pin_first`.

```{python}
code_link("code/corner_odds.py", "Corner odds to expected corners and corner supremacy")
```

A sample of the processed output for one Premier League weekend (7--8
February 2026):

```{python}
pin = load("sample_pinnacle_corners.csv")
pin["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(pin["Date"]).dt.strftime("%d %b")
pin_view = pin[["Date", "Home", "Away", "Corner Handicap", "Home Handicap Corners Odds",
                "Away Handicap Corners Odds", "Asian Corners Line", "Asian Corners O Odds",
                "Asian Corners U Odds", "corner_supremacy", "corner_total"]]
pin_view.columns = ["Date", "Home", "Away", "Handicap line", "Home odds", "Away odds",
                    "Totals line", "Over odds", "Under odds", "Corner Supremacy", "Corner Total"]
table(pin_view, floatfmt=".2f")
```

**How it's used.** Pinnacle's corner supremacy is the benchmark the
model has to beat. In the backtest, the model's predicted supremacy is
compared with Pinnacle's for each match. When the two disagree by a
specific threshold, a one unit bet is placed at Pinnacle's quoted odds
and settled on the actual corners. In the live model, the same
comparison flags value bets on upcoming fixtures.

**Why it's useful.** Pinnacle is widely regarded as the sharpest
bookmaker. It runs low margins, and is known for not restricting winning
customers, so its prices are the best estimate of the "true" market
view. Generally, a model that beats Pinnacle has found a real edge
rather than just a soft bookmaker. It is also the only bookmaker I have
an active account with so if I want to build a model that can be
profitable in real time it will need to beat Pinnacle lines.

Team and league names are spelled differently on the two sites, so a
name-mapping table joins them.

## 3. Data processing

The raw event data goes through three processing steps before any
analysis: working out the game state at every event, adding up the
minutes and corners each team had in each state, and flagging repeater
corners.

### Identifying game state at each match event

Each match's events are processed in time order, keeping a running count
of goals for each side. After every event the score gives the game
state: 0 = drawing, 1 = home winning, 2 = away winning. Recording where
the state *changes* marks the start and end of each spell of play at a
given scoreline.

Everton v Liverpool, 12 February 2025, with the running score and state
added:

```{python}
ev = load("example_match_events.csv")
ev.columns = ["Minute", "Team", "Event", "Home goals", "Away goals", "Game state"]
table(ev, floatfmt=".0f")
```

```{python}
code_link("code/gamestate.py#L21-L35", "Identifying game state: add_gamestate()")
```

### Minutes and corners in each game state

The total minutes each team spends in each game state is calculated
using the previous table. Every corner is then counted under the game
state it was won in, from the corner-taking team's point of view.

The result is one row per team per match. Two Premier League examples:

```{python}
ts = load("team_state_sample.csv")
ts["Opponent"] = ts["Away"].where(ts["Team"] == ts["Home"], ts["Home"])
ts_view = ts[["Team", "Opponent", "teamsup", "teamleadingmins", "teamdrawingmins", "teamlosingmins",
              "team_leading_corners", "team_drawing_corners", "team_losing_corners"]]
ts_view.columns = ["Team", "Opponent", "Supremacy", "Mins winning", "Mins drawing", "Mins losing",
                   "Corners winning", "Corners drawing", "Corners losing"]
ts_view = ts_view.astype({c: int for c in ts_view.columns[3:]})
table(ts_view, floatfmt=".2f")
```

Supremacy is the market's expected goal difference from each team's
point of view, so a positive number means the team was the pre-match
favourite.

This is a snapshot of the effect that game state and supremacy can have
on raw corner counts. Crystal Palace got 8 of their 9 corners during the
35 minutes they were losing. Tottenham, in a match they were big
favourites, got all 13 of their corners during the 52 minutes when they
were drawing or losing, and 0 in the 45 minutes they were winning.

These counts are aggregated at the league level in the analysis in
section four to find base rates for different combinations of game state
and supremacy. They also provide the context we need to make game state
and supremacy adjusted team ratings.

```{python}
code_link("code/gamestate.py#L38-L82", "Minutes in each state: add_gamestate_minutes()")
```

```{python}
code_link("code/gamestate.py#L85-L110", "Corners in each state: add_gamestate_corners()")
```

### Identifying repeaters

```{python}
rx = load("repeater_example.csv")
villa = rx[rx["Team"] == "Aston Villa"]
n_villa, n_villa_rep = len(villa), int(villa["Repeater"].sum())
```

A **repeater** is a corner that comes straight after another corner by
the same team. Repeaters are not statistically independent events: they
depend on the corner before them. A team can pick up two or more corners
in quick succession, but this is not a fair reflection of their
corner-generating strength. Over a small sample of games, a few of these
spells can skew a team's ratings.

Our minute-level event data allows us to identify repeaters. A corner is
flagged as a repeater if the previous event was also a corner, taken by
the same team, in the same half, and no more than one minute earlier.

All the corners from Aston Villa v Ipswich, 15 February 2025. Villa won
`{python} n_villa` corners, and `{python} n_villa_rep` of them were
repeaters:

```{python}
rx_view = rx[["Minute", "half", "Team", "Repeater"]].copy()
rx_view["Repeater"] = rx_view["Repeater"].map({0: "", 1: "TRUE"})
rx_view.columns = ["Minute", "Half", "Team", "Repeater"]
table(rx_view, floatfmt=".0f")
```

Repeaters are kept in the data but flagged, so each rating metric can
include or exclude them.

```{python}
code_link("code/repeaters.py#L13-L30", "Repeater detection: flag_repeaters()")
```

## 4. Analysis

### Game state affects corner rates

Teams that are behind attack more, so they win more corners. Teams that
are ahead tend to sit deeper and win fewer. The chart shows the home
side's share of all corners in each league, split by the game state at
the time.

```{python}
share = load("gs_home_corner_share.csv")
share = share[share["League"].isin(SHOWCASE_LEAGUES)]
p = share.assign(League=share["League"].map(pretty_league)).pivot(index="League", columns="home_match_state", values="home_share_pct")
p["spread"] = p["trailing"] - p["leading"]
p = p.sort_values("spread")

fig = go.Figure()
for league in p.index:  # connector line per league
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[p.loc[league, "leading"], p.loc[league, "trailing"]], y=[league, league],
                             mode="lines", line=dict(color="#d8d7d2", width=2),
                             showlegend=False, hoverinfo="skip"))
for col, label in [("leading", "Winning"), ("level", "Drawing"), ("trailing", "Losing")]:
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=p[col], y=p.index, mode="markers", name=f"Home {label.lower()}",
        marker=dict(size=9, color=STATE_COLORS[label], line=dict(color="white", width=1.5)),
        customdata=p["spread"],
        hovertemplate=f"<b>%{{y}}</b><br>Home {label.lower()}: %{{x:.1f}}%<br>Losing − winning: %{{customdata:.1f}} pts<extra></extra>",
    ))
fig.add_vline(x=50, line=dict(color=MUTED, width=1, dash="dot"))
fig.update_layout(height=26 * len(p) + 90, title="Home share of corners (%) by scoreline",
                  xaxis=dict(title=None, ticksuffix="%"), yaxis=dict(title=None, dtick=1, tickfont=dict(size=11)))
show(fig)
```

The size of the effect varies a lot by league: from about
`{python} f"{p['spread'].min():.0f}"` points in
`{python} p['spread'].idxmin()` to `{python} f"{p['spread'].max():.0f}"`
points in `{python} p['spread'].idxmax()`. Tactical cultures, the
prevalence of away fans and the role of dominant teams in each league
all play a part in explaining these disparities. **Any adjustment has to
be league-specific.**

### Short runs of games distort the picture

If every team's game state minutes were proportionate to their
underlying strength, game state biases less prevalent in the raw counts.
However, football matches are messy and chaotic and, especially over
short samples of games, teams spending disproportionate amounts of
minutes in different game states can distort corner rates.

The left panel shows how long each Premier League side *should* have
spent winning, drawing and losing over the first nine games of 2023/24,
based on the pre-match lines. The right panel shows how long they
actually did.

```{python}
m = load("epl_2324_state_minutes.csv")
m = m.rename(columns={"Leading": "Winning", "Level": "Drawing", "Trailing": "Losing"})
exp = m[m["basis"] == "Expected"].sort_values("Winning")
order = exp["Team"].tolist()
act = m[m["basis"] == "Actual"].set_index("Team").loc[order].reset_index()

fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, shared_yaxes=True, horizontal_spacing=0.04,
                    subplot_titles=("Expected (from betting lines)", "Actual"))
for col_i, df_ in enumerate([exp, act], start=1):
    for state in STATES:
        fig.add_trace(go.Bar(
            y=df_["Team"], x=df_[state], orientation="h", name=state,
            marker=dict(color=STATE_COLORS[state], line=dict(color="white", width=1)),
            legendgroup=state, showlegend=(col_i == 1),
            hovertemplate=f"<b>%{{y}}</b><br>{state}: %{{x:.0%}}<extra></extra>",
        ), row=1, col=col_i)
fig.update_layout(barmode="stack", height=560, bargap=0.2)
fig.update_xaxes(tickformat=".0%", range=[0, 1], dtick=0.25)
fig.update_annotations(font=dict(size=13, color=TEXT_2))
show(fig)
```

Several teams spent far more or far less time losing than their strength
implied. Their raw corner numbers could be inflated or deflated as a
result.

### Supremacy matters in every game state

Stronger teams win more corners, and that holds whether they're winning,
drawing or losing. To measure it, each league's team-matches are split
into 30 equal-sized buckets by pre-match supremacy, separately for home
and away sides. Within each bucket I calculate corners per minute in
each game state, then fit a line per state, weighted by the minutes
behind each bucket.

Pick a league:

```{python}
bk = load("gs_buckets_showcase.csv")
co = load("gs_coefficients.csv")
state_code = {0: "Drawing", 1: "Winning", 2: "Losing"}
bk["state"] = bk["team_gamestate"].map(state_code)
co["state"] = co["team_gamestate"].map(state_code)
default = "EnglandPremierLeague"

fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, shared_yaxes=True, horizontal_spacing=0.05, subplot_titles=("Home", "Away"))
league_of_trace = []
for lg in SHOWCASE_LEAGUES:
    for col_i, side in enumerate(["home", "away"], start=1):
        for state in STATES:
            d = bk[(bk["League"] == lg) & (bk["home_status"] == side) & (bk["state"] == state)]
            fit = co[(co["League"] == lg) & (co["home_status"] == side) & (co["state"] == state)].iloc[0]
            xs = np.array([d["adjsup_mean"].min(), d["adjsup_mean"].max()])
            fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
                x=d["adjsup_mean"], y=d["cpm"], mode="markers", name=state, legendgroup=state,
                showlegend=(col_i == 1), visible=(lg == default),
                marker=dict(color=STATE_COLORS[state], size=8, opacity=0.75, line=dict(color="white", width=1)),
                customdata=d[["mins"]],
                hovertemplate=f"{side.title()} · {state}<br>Supremacy %{{x:.2f}}<br>%{{y:.3f}} corners/min"
                              f"<br>%{{customdata[0]:,.0f}} mins<extra></extra>",
            ), row=1, col=col_i)
            fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
                x=xs, y=fit["Intercept"] + fit["Coefficient"] * xs, mode="lines", legendgroup=state,
                showlegend=False, visible=(lg == default), line=dict(color=STATE_COLORS[state], width=2),
                hovertemplate=f"{side.title()} · {state} (fitted)<br>Supremacy %{{x:.2f}}: %{{y:.3f}} corners/min<extra></extra>",
            ), row=1, col=col_i)
            league_of_trace += [lg, lg]

buttons = [dict(label=pretty_league(lg), method="update",
                args=[{"visible": [t == lg for t in league_of_trace]}])
           for lg in SHOWCASE_LEAGUES]
fig.update_layout(
    height=460, title="Corners per minute vs pre-match supremacy",
    updatemenus=[dict(buttons=buttons, active=SHOWCASE_LEAGUES.index(default), x=1, xanchor="right",
                      y=1.1, yanchor="bottom", bgcolor="white", bordercolor="#d8d7d2")],
)
fig.update_xaxes(title="Team supremacy (goals)")
fig.update_yaxes(title="Corners per minute", rangemode="tozero", row=1, col=1)
fig.update_annotations(font=dict(size=13, color=TEXT_2))
show(fig)
```

Each dot is one supremacy bucket, and hovering shows how many minutes
are in that bucket. Across all leagues, losing sides win corners fastest
and winning sides slowest, and the lines rise with supremacy. Together,
the six lines give an *expected* corner rate for any combination of
home/away, game state and supremacy, which drives the adjusted corner
values later in this section.


### Repeaters are stable across teams

Each dot below is one team, showing the share of its corners that were
repeaters (defined in section 3):

```{python}
rt = load("repeaters_by_team.csv")
rt["League"] = rt["League"].map(pretty_league)
rt = rt.sort_values("League", ascending=False)
rep_lo, rep_hi = (rt["repeater_rate"].quantile([0.05, 0.95]) * 100).round(0).astype(int)
fig = go.Figure(go.Box(
    x=rt["repeater_rate"], y=rt["League"], orientation="h", boxpoints="all", jitter=0.4, pointpos=0,
    marker=dict(color=ACCENT, size=6, opacity=0.6), line=dict(color=MUTED, width=1), fillcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)",
    customdata=rt[["Team", "matches"]],
    hovertemplate="<b>%{customdata[0]}</b><br>Repeater rate: %{x:.1%}<br>Matches: %{customdata[1]}<extra></extra>",
    showlegend=False))
fig.update_layout(title="Repeater rate by team (teams with 100+ matches)", height=620,
                  xaxis=dict(tickformat=".0%"), yaxis=dict(title=None))
show(fig)
```

The rate is stable at around 13--15% across leagues and across teams
within each league: 90% of the `{python} len(rt)` teams fall between
`{python} rep_lo`% and `{python} rep_hi`%. So removing repeaters doesn't
penalise any particular style of play. It just removes correlated noise.

### Adjusted corner values

Each corner is valued as the *average* corner rate divided by the rate
we'd *expect* given the context it was won in:

$$
\text{value} = \frac{\text{average rate}_{\text{home/away}}}{\text{expected rate}(\text{home/away},\ \text{game state},\ \text{supremacy})}
$$

A corner won where corners are usually rare (a big underdog, while
winning) is worth more than 1. One won where they're usually plentiful
(a big favourite chasing the game) is worth less than 1. Repeaters are
worth 0.

**Case study: Rayo Vallecano 1--2 Barcelona, 27 August 2024.** Barcelona
went in as 0.77-goal favourites. Rayo scored in the 9th minute,
Barcelona equalised in the 60th and won it with an 82nd-minute goal.

```{python}
cs = load("case_study_corners.csv")
cs["Repeater"] = cs["Repeater"].map({0: "", 1: "TRUE"})
tbl = cs[["Minute", "Team", "team_state", "Repeater", "expected_rate", "avg_rate", "adj_corner_value"]].copy()
tbl.columns = ["Min", "Team", "Team state", "Repeater", "Expected rate", "Average rate", "Value"]
table(tbl, floatfmt=".3f")
```

```{python}
tot = cs.groupby("Team").agg(raw=("Minute", "size"), adj=("adj_corner_value", "sum"))
rv, ba = tot.loc["Rayo Vallecano"], tot.loc["Barcelona"]
```

-   **Drawing:** Rayo corners are worth
    `{python} f"{cs[(cs.Team=='Rayo Vallecano')&(cs.team_state=='Drawing')].adj_corner_value.max():.2f}"`
    and Barcelona's
    `{python} f"{cs[(cs.Team=='Barcelona')&(cs.team_state=='Drawing')&(cs.Repeater=='')].adj_corner_value.max():.2f}"`.
    The gap reflects the difference in team strength alone.
-   **Rayo winning:** a Rayo corner is worth
    `{python} f"{cs[(cs.Team=='Rayo Vallecano')&(cs.team_state=='Winning')].adj_corner_value.max():.2f}"`,
    because an underdog protecting a lead rarely wins corners.
    Barcelona's are worth
    `{python} f"{cs[(cs.Team=='Barcelona')&(cs.team_state=='Losing')].adj_corner_value.max():.2f}"`,
    because a favourite chasing the game typically wins more corners.
-   **Barcelona winning:** the game-state and supremacy effects roughly
    cancel out, and both sides' corners are worth close to 1.

Raw corners: Rayo Vallecano
**`{python} f"{rv.raw:.0f}"`--`{python} f"{ba.raw:.0f}"`** Barcelona.

Adjusted: Rayo Vallecano
**`{python} f"{rv.adj:.2f}"`--`{python} f"{ba.adj:.2f}"`** Barcelona.

Once you account for the relative strength of the teams and Barcelona
chasing the game for more than 50 minutes, Rayo's corner performance
looks more impressive than Barcelona's, even with two of their repeater
corners removed.

```{python}
code_link("code/adjusted_values.py", "Buckets, fitted lines and adjusted values")
```

Because supremacy is stripped out of each corner's value, a team's
rating no longer depends much on *who* it has played. That means shorter
rating windows can be used, so changes of manager or personnel show up
sooner. It also means promoted and relegated teams carry their ratings
between divisions without special handling. The prediction model then
adds supremacy back in as a separate input, taken from the upcoming
match's betting lines.

## 5. Building and testing a predictive model

### Adjusted ratings make better predictions

Team attack and defence ratings are built as rolling averages over the
last *N* games, using four metrics:

-   **raw**: raw corner counts
-   **nr**: raw counts with repeaters removed
-   **adj**: adjusted values
-   **adj_nr**: adjusted values with repeaters removed

A rating of 1.00 means a team wins corners at the league-average rate
for that venue. The table shows current attack ratings for a sample of
Premier League teams on all four metrics, over a 25-game window:

```{python}
cr = load("epl_current_ratings.csv")
cr_asof = pd.to_datetime(cr[["home_rating_as_of", "away_rating_as_of"]].stack()).max()
metrics = ["raw", "nr", "adj", "adj_nr"]
cr_view = pd.concat([
    cr.pivot(index="Team", columns="metric", values=f"{side}_corner_attack_rating")[metrics]
      .add_prefix(f"{side.capitalize()} ")
    for side in ["home", "away"]], axis=1)
cr_view = cr_view.loc[cr["Team"].unique()].reset_index()
table(cr_view, floatfmt=".2f")
```

On raw counts, Man City, Liverpool, Arsenal and Chelsea look like the
league's strongest corner-winning sides at home, at around 1.15 to 1.30.
On the adjusted metrics they drop back to roughly 0.9 to 1.1, because
most of their raw advantage is what their supremacy would already
predict. Bournemouth and Newcastle stay near the top at home on every
metric, so their corner numbers are not just a product of being
favourites. Ratings as of `{python} f"{cr_asof.day} {cr_asof:%B %Y}"`.

Each set of ratings, together with match supremacy, feeds an OLS model
that predicts each side's corners for matches in the test dataset. The
chart shows the out-of-sample R² improvement over raw counts, for each
window length.

```{python}
piv = rb.pivot_table(index=["side", "window_size"], columns="metric", values="r2_test").reset_index()
for mt in ["nr", "adj", "adj_nr"]:
    piv[f"d_{mt}"] = (piv[mt] / piv["raw"] - 1) * 100

metric_colors = {"nr": MUTED, "adj": "#86b6ef", "adj_nr": ACCENT}
fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, shared_yaxes=True, horizontal_spacing=0.05,
                    subplot_titles=("Home corners", "Away corners"))
for col_i, side in enumerate(["home", "away"], start=1):
    d = piv[piv["side"] == side]
    for mt in ["nr", "adj", "adj_nr"]:
        fig.add_trace(go.Bar(
            x=d["window_size"].astype(str), y=d[f"d_{mt}"], name=mt, legendgroup=mt, showlegend=(col_i == 1),
            marker=dict(color=metric_colors[mt]),
            customdata=np.c_[d[mt], d["raw"]],
            hovertemplate=f"{mt}, window %{{x}}<br>R² %{{customdata[0]:.4f}} vs raw %{{customdata[1]:.4f}}<br>%{{y:+.1f}}% vs raw<extra></extra>",
        ), row=1, col=col_i)
fig.update_layout(barmode="group", height=400, title="Out-of-sample R², % change vs raw corner ratings")
fig.update_xaxes(title="Rating window (games)")
fig.update_yaxes(ticksuffix="%", zeroline=True, zerolinecolor=MUTED, row=1, col=1)
fig.update_annotations(font=dict(size=13, color=TEXT_2))
show(fig)

best = rb[(rb["metric"] == "adj_nr") & (rb["window_size"] == 25)].set_index("side")
raw25 = rb[(rb["metric"] == "raw") & (rb["window_size"] == 25)].set_index("side")
```

The adjusted metrics beat raw counts at every window length on both
sides. The gain is largest for home corners, which are the most
sensitive to game state. Removing repeaters from raw counts (nr) makes
little difference on its own; almost all of the gain comes from the
game-state and supremacy adjustment.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
R² values of around 0.1 are normal here. Match-level corner counts are
dominated by Poisson-like randomness, so no pre-match model explains
most of the variance. What matters for betting is whether the model
beats the market's estimate, which is tested next.
:::

### Beating the market

The model's predicted corner supremacy (home minus away) is compared
with Pinnacle's implied corner supremacy for every priced match in
2024/25 and 2025/26. The prediction model is fitted only on earlier
seasons, and ratings use only matches played before each fixture. When
the two differ by 0.5 corners or more, a 1-unit bet goes on the side the
model prefers, at Pinnacle's price. Every bet is settled on actual raw
corners.

```{python}
bg = bets_g.copy()
bg["combo"] = bg["metric"] + " · " + bg["window_size"].astype(str)
bg = bg.sort_values("roi")
fig = go.Figure(go.Bar(
    x=bg["roi"], y=bg["combo"], orientation="h",
    marker=dict(color=np.where(bg["roi"] >= 0, POS, NEG)),
    customdata=bg[["n_bets", "total_pnl"]],
    text=(bg["roi"] * 100).map("{:+.1f}%".format), textposition="outside", textfont=dict(color=TEXT_2),
    hovertemplate="<b>%{y}</b><br>ROI %{x:.2%}<br>%{customdata[0]:,} bets · %{customdata[1]:+.1f} units<extra></extra>",
))
fig.update_layout(title="Corner handicap ROI by rating set (metric · window)", height=360,
                  xaxis=dict(tickformat=".0%", range=[0, bg["roi"].max() * 1.25]), yaxis=dict(title=None))
show(fig)
```

All `{python} n_combos` adjusted rating sets are profitable in the
handicap market, at between
`{python} f"{roi_lo:.1f}"`--`{python} f"{roi_hi:.1f}"`% ROI.

### **How the edge scales**

Raising the minimum threshold before betting shows the balance between
ROI and volume. We are interested in finding the threshold that
maximises units won.

```{python}
cv = load("ev_variant_peak_pnl_curves.csv")
cv = cv[cv["rule_family"] == "diff_sup"]
cv = cv[cv["n_bets"] >= 50]
peak = cv.loc[cv["total_pnl"].idxmax()]
breakeven = cv[cv["total_pnl"] > 0]["threshold"].min()

fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, horizontal_spacing=0.14, subplot_titles=("Total profit (units)", "ROI"),
                    specs=[[{"secondary_y": True}, {"secondary_y": True}]])
hover = "Edge ≥ %{x:.2f} corners<br>%{customdata[0]:,} bets<br>Profit %{customdata[1]:+.1f}u · ROI %{customdata[2]:.1%}<extra></extra>"
cd = cv[["n_bets", "total_pnl", "roi"]]
# Bet volume as bars behind each line. Plotly draws the secondary axis on top, so the bars take the
# primary axis (shown on the right) and the lines the secondary axis (shown on the left).
for col_i, ycol in ((1, "total_pnl"), (2, "roi")):
    fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=cv["threshold"], y=cv["n_bets"], name="Bets", legendgroup="bets", showlegend=(col_i == 1),
                         marker=dict(color=MUTED, opacity=0.25), customdata=cd, hovertemplate=hover),
                  row=1, col=col_i, secondary_y=False)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=cv["threshold"], y=cv[ycol], mode="lines", line=dict(color=ACCENT, width=2),
                             customdata=cd, hovertemplate=hover, showlegend=False),
                  row=1, col=col_i, secondary_y=True)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[peak["threshold"]], y=[peak["total_pnl"]], mode="markers+text",
                         marker=dict(color=ACCENT, size=9, line=dict(color="white", width=2)),
                         text=[f"peak {peak['total_pnl']:.0f}u at ≥{peak['threshold']:.2f}"], textposition="top right",
                         textfont=dict(color=TEXT_2, size=11), hoverinfo="skip", showlegend=False),
              row=1, col=1, secondary_y=True)
fig.update_xaxes(title="Minimum model–market disagreement (corners)")
fig.update_yaxes(side="left", tickmode="auto", zeroline=True, zerolinecolor=MUTED, gridcolor=GRID, secondary_y=True)
fig.update_yaxes(tickformat=".0%", row=1, col=2, secondary_y=True)
fig.update_yaxes(side="right", showgrid=False, zeroline=False, tickformat=",", rangemode="tozero",
                 title=dict(text="Bets", font=dict(color=TEXT_2, size=11)), secondary_y=False)
fig.update_layout(height=400, bargap=0.15, legend=dict(orientation="h", y=-0.3, x=0))
fig.update_annotations(font=dict(size=13, color=TEXT_2))
show(fig)
```

Betting every match loses money. Once the model disagrees by
`{python} f"{breakeven:.2f}"` corners or more, profit becomes positive.
It peaks at **`{python} f"{peak['total_pnl']:.0f}"` units** at a
`{python} f"{peak['threshold']:.2f}"`-corner threshold. ROI rises
broadly as the threshold tightens, which is the pattern you'd expect if
the edge is real. Above about 1.2 corners it gets noisy, because there
are only a few hundred bets left. The 0.5 threshold used above was
chosen on this same data, so treat the peak as optimistic. The steady
rise in ROI is the more reliable evidence.

**The totals market is different.** The same ratings were backtested
against Pinnacle's corner over/under lines, and every metric/window
combination lost money. My working hypothesis is that game state shifts
*which side* wins the corners much more than it changes *how many*
corners there are in total, so correcting for it helps the handicap
market and doesn't help totals.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
This is a backtest over roughly two seasons on historical prices. Bets
aren't guaranteed to have been available at those odds or stakes, and
results vary by league: some are consistently profitable, others
negative. See the [methodology](methodology.qmd) page for caveats.
:::

## 6. Running the model in real time

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
This section is being written.
:::

Each day the pipeline rebuilds the ratings, predicts corners for
upcoming fixtures and joins the predictions to Pinnacle's live corner
handicap prices. A bet is flagged when the model's corner supremacy
differs from Pinnacle's by at least 0.5 corners, the threshold tested
in section 5, or when the expected value on one side is at least 8%.
A sample from one weekend in September 2026:

```{python}
ps = load("predictions_sample.csv")
home_bet = ps["value_bet"] == "home"
bet_line = ps["Corner Handicap"].where(home_bet, -ps["Corner Handicap"])
ps_view = pd.DataFrame({
    "Date": pd.to_datetime(ps["Date"]).dt.strftime("%d %b"),
    "League": ps["League"].map(pretty_league),
    "Match": ps["Home"] + " v " + ps["Away"],
    "Model sup": ps["predicted_supremacy"],
    "Pinnacle sup": ps["corner_supremacy"],
    "Difference": ps["diff_sup"],
    "Bet": (ps["Home"].where(home_bet, ps["Away"]) + " " + bet_line.map(lambda v: f"{v:+.1f}" if v else "0.0")).where(ps["value_bet"].notna(), "–"),
    "Odds": ps["Home Handicap Corners Odds"].where(home_bet, ps["Away Handicap Corners Odds"]),
    "P(cover)": ps["p_cover_home"].where(home_bet, ps["p_cover_away"]),
    "EV": ps["ev_home"].where(home_bet, ps["ev_away"]),
})
no_bet = ps["value_bet"].isna()
ps_view[["Odds", "P(cover)", "EV"]] = ps_view[["Odds", "P(cover)", "EV"]].astype(object)
ps_view.loc[no_bet, ["Odds", "P(cover)", "EV"]] = "–"
ps_view.loc[~no_bet, "Odds"] = ps_view.loc[~no_bet, "Odds"].map(lambda v: f"{v:.2f}")
for c in ["P(cover)", "EV"]:
    ps_view.loc[~no_bet, c] = ps_view.loc[~no_bet, c].map(lambda v: f"{v:.0%}")
table(ps_view, floatfmt=".2f")
```

Supremacy is home corners minus away corners, and the difference is the
model minus Pinnacle. P(cover) is the model's probability that the bet
wins, with each side's corners treated as an independent Poisson count
around its prediction, and EV is the expected return per unit staked at
Pinnacle's odds. Where the model and the market agree, as in Napoli v
Bologna or Inter Milan v Udinese, there's no bet.

### Limitations and next steps

-   **Match length is estimated.** The source data doesn't record
    stoppage time, so match length is taken as the later of 97 minutes
    and the last recorded event. Better data would improve the minute
    counts.
-   **Other in-game factors aren't modelled yet.** Red cards and the
    *timing* of each game state (the effects grow as the match goes on)
    are obvious next adjustments.
-   **Out-of-game factors aren't modelled either.** Manager changes,
    transfers and end-of-season motivation aren't captured beyond what
    the rolling window picks up.
-   **No player-level data.** Lineup-aware ratings would help with
    injuries and rotation.
-   **Data quality.** Some team names are split across different
    spellings in lower leagues, which affects rolling windows for the
    teams involved. Three leagues are excluded until they're given
    league/tier context.
-   **Bet sizing.** All backtests use flat 1-unit stakes. Kelly-style
    sizing based on the size of the disagreement is untested.
